breastfeedingNote: Feed on demand — newborns often cluster-feed, especially in the evening. Frequency matters more than a strict schedule at this stage.
Feeds may start to space out slightly as your baby's stomach capacity grows. Continue feeding on demand.
A more predictable rhythm often emerges, though every baby's pattern varies. Growth spurts (commonly around 3 weeks and 6 weeks) can temporarily increase feeding frequency.
Feeding sessions often become more efficient (shorter but just as effective) as your baby gets better at nursing.
Milk (breast milk or formula) is still the primary source of nutrition through this stage, even after solids begin.
solidsNote: Most babies show readiness signs for solid foods somewhere in this window (good head control, sitting with support, interest in food) — but milk remains the main source of nutrition, with solids introduced gradually as a complement, not a replacement.

breastfeedingNote: Milk feeds may reduce slightly in frequency as solid food intake increases, but milk still provides the majority of nutrition and calories at this stage.
solidsNote: Solid meals are typically offered 2-3 times per day alongside milk feeds. Textures can progress from purees to soft finger foods depending on your baby's readiness and your pediatrician's guidance.

breastfeedingNote: Milk remains an important part of nutrition, though solid foods now make up a larger share of daily intake.
solidsNote: Most babies are eating 3 meals a day plus 1-2 snacks, with a widening variety of textures and finger foods.

formulaAmountOz: Whole milk typically replaces formula/breast milk as the main drink, alongside water
breastfeedingNote: Continued breastfeeding beyond 12 months is supported by the WHO and AAP for as long as mother and baby wish to continue, alongside a full diet of solid foods.
solidsNote: Most toddlers are eating a version of family meals by this stage, with attention to choking-hazard foods (whole grapes, nuts, hard raw vegetables) still needed.
